item.title: Partitioning and Merging in Phase Unwrapping: A Systematic Review of Methods and Evidence
item.description: arXiv:2611.33194v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Phase unwrapping underlies radar interferometry, magnetic resonance imaging and optical metrology. When an image is too large or too difficult to unwrap in one piece, many methods cut it into units, unwrap each unit, and merge the results. To our knowledge, no systematic review had brought these partitioned methods together. This review gathers them, for two-dimensional images and three-dimensional volumes. It describes how the units are built: fixed tiles, adaptive tiles, regions computed from the data, or pieces imposed by the acquisition, such as subapertures, slices and scenes. It then classifies how the units are merged, in four classes: after each unit is unwrapped, through one integer per jump-free region, during the solve, or through an external reference. Three findings stand out: building the units and merging them are two separate decisions; the merging rule decides whether the merged phase stays congruent with the measured one; and most tests change both decisions at once, so few results show which one helps. We state what a study can report to support a claim on memory, speed or accuracy. Our aim is to document the methods, not to rank them. Following PRISMA 2020, four bibliographic databases (OpenAlex, IEEE Xplore, Web of Science and Scopus), searched on 1 October 2026, returned 1,800 records. After removing duplicates, screening titles and abstracts, adding a citation search and reading 298 full texts, we included 149 studies, published from 1987 to 2026. The review was not registered and received no specific funding.
item.dc:creator: Antoine Moevus, Max Mignotte

item.title: Diagnostically Meaningful, Privacy-aware Synthetic Chest CT via Class-Conditional Latent Sampling in Diffusion Autoencoders
item.description: arXiv:2611.33234v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large, well-annotated datasets are essential for developing medical artificial intelligence models, yet data sharing is often restricted by privacy regulations. Synthetic images may help address this limitation if they preserve diagnostic information while reducing the risk of reproducing patient data. We developed a diffusion autoencoder-based framework for class-conditional synthetic chest CT generation that incorporates latent-space distance filtering to reduce the likelihood of regenerating training samples. A diffusion autoencoder was trained on the public RSNA 2020 Pulmonary Embolism (PE) dataset. PE-positive and PE-negative images were synthesized by sampling latent representations from class-specific kernel density estimates. Samples with a nearest-neighbor latent-space distance below a predefined threshold were rejected. To assess diagnostic utility, ResNet-50 classifiers were trained across 10 independent runs using real, synthetic, or mixed real-synthetic datasets. Performance was evaluated on a held-out real test set using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), with DeLong 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Models trained on synthetic data achieved an AUC of 0.862 (95% CI, 0.851-0.874), only slightly lower than models trained on real data (AUC = 0.872, 95% CI, 0.861-0.883) and mixed real-synthetic data (AUC = 0.865, 95% CI, 0.855-0.876). These differences were statistically significant (p < 0.05) but small in absolute terms. A nearest-neighbor copy-detection analysis of 38,000 synthetic slices found no direct copies of real training images. These findings indicate that the synthetic CT images preserve diagnostically meaningful information for image-level PE classification while incorporating measures intended to enhance privacy awareness and reduce similarity to real patient data.
item.dc:creator: Johannes B. Thalhammer, Kacper Og\'orek, Tina Dorosti, Sebastian Peterhansl, Daniel Frey, Zijin Huang, Theresa Hiu, Tobias Lasser, Daniela Pfeiffer, Franz Pfeiffer, Florian Schaff

item.title: Conformal Risk Control for Sentinel-1 Flood Maps under Event Shift and Local Recalibration
item.description: arXiv:2611.33235v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Conformal Risk Control (CRC) selects a threshold to limit missed labeled positives under exchangeability, but low omission risk can come at the cost of an excessively large flood map. We examine this trade-off with a frozen bi-temporal Sentinel-1 predictor, 403 expert-labeled source groups, and ten evaluable leave-one-event-out folds. At a target risk of 0.10, source-calibrated thresholds produce mean group losses of 0.1726 in Somalia and 0.1985 in Nigeria (four groups). The other eight folds select zero thresholds, labeling every valid pixel as flooded; their excess predicted area is 3.15-20.55 times the labeled positive area. Local threshold recalibration is feasible in 559 of 570 scheduled splits. The equal-event frequency of meeting the observed risk target with a positive threshold is 0.95% at ten labeled groups and 8.00% at twenty, using different predefined event pools. At fifty groups, exploratory recalibration meets both conditions in 24/30 Paraguay splits and none in India or the United States. Labels include permanent water, so the loss does not isolate newly flooded land. The results show why omission risk should be reported alongside mapped area, calibration feasibility, and event-specific outcomes.
item.dc:creator: Izzath Nisfer, Rahim Iqbal, Shazan Shaheed, Asfi Ahamed, Muhammadu Ilham, Dileesha Manamperi, Thimira Sahan, Sandareka Wickramanayake

item.title: NeuroRefine: Six-Head MLP Content Conditioning and Qwen Refinement for Faithful fMRI Decoding
item.description: arXiv:2611.33309v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructing seen images from fMRI has advanced through diffusion models, but the current state-of-the-art Brain-IT pipeline still has a lossy bottleneck: its low-level branch outlines the figure well, yet the diffusion model that follows frequently mispaints colour, object identity and layout. We move one step backward and condition the refiner directly on the fMRI-derived low-level image, using six one-hidden-layer MLP heads (scene, main-subject category, count, colour, object, layout) to predict the content prompt that guides a frozen Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 model. On the 930 shared NSD concepts, scored with Brain-IT's own metric code on the same ground truth, NeuroRefine reaches a CLIP image cosine of 0.755 against 0.735 for Brain-IT enhanced and produces markedly sharper images, while the saturated 2-way identification is unchanged. The low-level image supplies an explicit spatial prior rather than a lossless layout: refinement trades some layout agreement (0.541 against 0.638) for semantic fidelity and texture. We then show that the standard panel is multi-factor: a high PixCorr can coexist with completely different content, so we read the low-level and semantic factors separately and quantify where they disagree. Finally, we trace the cortical sources of the prompt heads across subjects and report their causal lesion profile and the fMRI noise ceiling. Direction errors are left to future work.
item.dc:creator: Runqi Xu, Vince D. Calhoun

item.title: PICE: Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution Toward Self-Evolving Medical Image Recognition
item.description: arXiv:2611.33626v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Medical image classifiers in clinical practice must continually evolve to accommodate emerging disease categories while maintaining reliable classification of existing conditions. This is challenging because privacy and data-sharing restrictions limit access to historical patient data, while assigning dedicated capacity to each new diagnostic task causes linear model growth. Effective evolution requires preserving prior disease knowledge without retaining historical images while expanding model capacity only when necessary. To this end, we propose PICE, a Prototype-Informed Conditional Model Evolution framework organized around what to preserve, when evolution is needed, and how that evolution is realized. PICE preserves prior disease knowledge in a prototype-statistical memory. For each incoming task, it assesses compatibility with historical references reconstructed from memory, reusing the closest adapter when compatibility is sufficient and instantiating a new one when evolution is required. PICE then realizes evolution by updating the memory and recalibrating the unified classifier with Gaussian pseudo features, thereby integrating new knowledge into the cumulative diagnostic space. During inference, memory-derived similarities guide task-agnostic adapter selection and fusion, enabling prediction over all learned disease categories. Experiments on Skin8, Kvasir-V2, and Path16 demonstrate the effectiveness of PICE across diverse clinical scenarios. On Skin8, PICE achieves a 7.60\% improvement in accuracy over the SOTA method on new tasks, while maintaining 71.10\% accuracy on previous tasks. It also reduces additional learnable parameters by 18.51\%. These results indicate that PICE improves classification while balancing knowledge retention, adaptation, and parameter growth, supporting continual model evolution as new diagnostic categories emerge without access to historical images.
item.dc:creator: Yifan Zhu, Jie Xu, Zeju Li, Yi Guo, Yuanyuan Wang

item.title: Interpreting Speckle Effects Through Neuron Interventions
item.description: arXiv:2611.33632v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speckle, the multiplicative noise inherent to synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging, reduces the performance of pretrained SAR models. We use interpretability methods to examine its effects inside pretrained vision models. We identify neurons that respond selectively to speckle and test whether correcting their activations improves reconstruction. We study SARMAE, an Earth observation model pretrained on a million-scale SAR dataset. Synthetic scenes with known reflectivity allow us to measure recovery precisely. The model contains 38 speckle-selective neurons that track speckle's value distribution. Restoring these neurons to their clean values does not improve reconstruction. Activation patching across layers shows that the first MLP has the largest restoration and injection effects. Within this layer, a different set of 64 neurons recovers 44.1\% of the correlation loss on held-out scenes. When the speckle-selective neurons are held at their noisy values, 96.5\% of this gain remains, while holding the values of three decoder heads removes 37.4\%. In an ImageNet-pretrained MAE, restoration is most effective in the third MLP block. On manipulated Sentinel-1 and Capella images, the same 64 neurons also improve reconstruction, whereas for land-cover classification, only restoring the entire first MLP yields a clear gain. The neurons that respond most to speckle are therefore not the ones the model uses to recover the scene.
item.dc:creator: Shubham K. Singh, Hare Krishna

item.title: Evaluating Cine and Tagged MRI-to-Speech Synthesis with Complementary Metrics and MRI-Free Controls
item.description: arXiv:2611.33786v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Relating tongue motion measured with dynamic MRI to the speech it produces could inform rehabilitation after glossectomy. Prior studies have translated cine or tagged MRI into log-mel spectrograms and used the two-dimensional Pearson correlation between predicted and recorded spectrograms (Corr2D) to quantify the acoustic information captured by each imaging modality. However, Corr2D has not been calibrated against MRI-free predictors that preserve basic acoustic structure. Our contribution is an evaluation framework for speech synthesis from cine MRI, tagged MRI and their combination; the synthesis network is held fixed. On identical leave-one-subject-out folds, we compare four trained input configurations with two MRI-free controls: a static mean-spectrum baseline and a time-aligned cohort template. Across 44 subjects (18 after glossectomy) producing two utterances, the cohort template, which never sees an MRI, reached a Corr2D of 0.745 and 0.664. The static baseline, which contains no timing, reached 87 to 89% of that score. No trained configuration outperformed the template on Corr2D, a cepstral distance or ESTOI; seven of the eight fell significantly short on Corr2D. For cine MRI this held across three positional encodings, an encoder temporal-attention module and a training objective matched to the metric. Cine and tagged MRI differed consistently within subjects, although the direction depended on the metric. Absolute Corr2D alone therefore does not show that a model recovers acoustics from the MRI. The two controls are a reusable method: any study can compute them from its own training recordings, so a model's margin over them measures what its images contribute.
item.dc:creator: Karlo Vrancic, Fangxu Xing, Jiachen Zhuo, Maureen Stone, Jerry L. Prince, Jonghye Woo

item.title: SpiderSkel: Sub-Pixel Multi-Tangent 2D Skeletonization from Inscribed-Disc Geometry
item.description: arXiv:2611.33805v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Skeletonization reduces a binary shape to a compact medial representation, but pixel-grid discretization perturbs the boundary-contact geometry underlying the medial axis, creating tension among connectivity, reconstruction fidelity, and skeleton compactness. SpiderSkel is a family of training-free two-dimensional skeletonization methods built on multi-tangent inscribed-disc geometry. A tie-aware exact Euclidean distance transform retains tied nearest boundary sites rather than collapsing them to a single label; medial candidates are localised to sub-pixel positions from the inscribed disc's tangent contacts, filtered by the angular span of those contacts, and completed by connectivity-aware refinement. Across nineteen public benchmarks comprising 11,323 images of shapes, retinal vessels, cracks and roads, and document images, a single operating point fixed across datasets yields skeletons that, on every image, have exact skeleton topology under the component/hole certificate, remain fully connected, and have exact per-object reconstruction topology. The three SpiderSkel variants are the only evaluated methods to satisfy all three properties across every category; within each category, every variant is Pareto-optimal with respect to all twenty-two baselines in strict sub-pixel reconstruction Dice versus reduction rate. Incremental engines for all three variants reproduce the skeleton of a complete recomputation exactly across 23,040 verified edit steps, with median update latencies of 15.4-18.1 ms per foreground edit and 4.3-4.4 ms per canvas edit, and speedups reaching 33.0-fold on canvas edits.
item.dc:creator: Zhexian Zhou, Lian Ren, Xiao Feng, Sebastian Scherer

item.title: PRISM: Perceptual Rate-Controllable Extreme Image Compression with Visual State-Space Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.33839v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Generative codecs built on pretrained diffusion priors achieve high perceptual quality at ultra-low bitrates (below 0.05 bpp). However, most methods still require a separate model for each bitrate, and offer no control over the amount of detail synthesized. Their rate efficiency also depends on the entropy model, where Mamba-based state-space models (SSMs) have recently improved autoregressive context modeling. However, conventional SSM scans are not aligned with the decoding order, and each decoding pass restarts from an empty state, discarding context accumulated in previous passes. We propose PRISM, an extreme image compression method that addresses these limitations. A single model provides two continuous controls: a rate knob that traverses the rate-distortion curve and a realism knob that adjusts the level of detail synthesized. Its visual state-space (VSS) context model introduces a decode-order-aligned (DOA) scan, which predicts each latent from a state that summarizes all decoded context, and cross-tap state carry, which initializes each tap with a summary of the previous one. Experiments show that PRISM outperforms both variable-rate and fixed-rate codecs, requiring on average 22% less bitrate than the strongest baseline at equal FID while also achieving higher PSNR.
item.dc:creator: Md Adnan Faisal Hossain, Fengqing Zhu

item.title: Weakly Conditioned Diffusion Model Augmentation for Prostate Segmentation
item.description: arXiv:2611.34230v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models for prostate MRI segmentation often struggle to generalize when trained on limited heterogeneous data, leading to boundary errors and over-segmentation. We present an augmentation framework using mask-conditioned synthetic and diverse T2-weighted MRI volumes to improve boundary precision and reduce over-segmentation. We employ a 2.5D weakly mask-conditioned denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) via channel concatenation. The diffusion model conditions on stacks of adjacent binary masks from training folds. The model generates T2 volumes consistent with the conditioning anatomy while diversifying tissue appearance. We evaluate the proposed approach on two cohorts of data: (i) the LUND probe cohort (n=432) for strategy selection and training nnU-Net from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix, and (ii) the Medical Segmentation Decathlon (MSD) prostate cohort (n=32) evaluated with a 20% synthetic data mix. For the LUND cohort, we found that training an nnU-Net model from scratch with a 23% synthetic data mix reduced the mean false-positive voxels per case from 11,102 (baseline) to 10,757. On the MSD cohort, the augmented model with a 20% synthetic mix achieved a mean cross-validated Dice of 0.9094, improving over the baseline (0.8935) by 1.59 percentage points and reducing mean false-positive voxels by 23.1% (4,201 to 3,229). Experimental results on both these cohorts suggest that mask-conditioned DDPM augmentation can reduce over-segmentation errors and improve boundary adherence in data-constrained settings.
item.dc:creator: Chibike Ugbam, Muhammad Bilal, Jia Wu, Shafaq Murad, Rizwan Qureshi, Hazrat Ali

item.title: Real-time Food Recipe Generation with Mobile Deep Learning and Large Language Model
item.description: arXiv:2611.33177v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Finding recipes that match available kitchen ingredients can be cumbersome and inefficient. This paper addresses this challenge by developing a mobile application that generates tailored food recipes based on ingredients identified using a mobile camera. Leveraging deep learning and large language model (LLM), our system offers a seamless and efficient solution for real-time recipe generation. By integrating deep learning for accurate ingredient recognition with LLM for generating detailed and practical recipes, our approach ensures users receive precise cooking instructions based on actual ingredients on hand. Extensive dataset augmentation and model training have resulted in a robust system capable of high performance. Experimental results demonstrate that EfficientNet, used for food recognition, offers a balance of accuracy and computational efficiency, making it ideal for mobile applications. This dual-approach method enhances the cooking experience, reduces food waste, and provides a comprehensive, real-time tool for everyday cooking needs, bridging a significant gap in current food recommendation systems.
item.dc:creator: Wei Jun Leung, Mun Hong Lee, Joo Wee Quek, Desmond Loy, Yifei Wang, Yan Ning Ang, Pai Chet Ng, Kan Chen, Jeannie Lee

item.title: Frame geometry, fascicle extrapolation and leaderboard overfitting in muscle ultrasound
item.description: arXiv:2611.33539v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Automated readings of pennation angle, fascicle length and muscle thickness from B-mode ultrasound depend on the geometry of the stored frame and on how fascicles that leave the image are extended, and challenge entries add settings chosen on a small public leaderboard. This study measures all three in one entry of the UMUD Challenge, which scored 309 frames from six screen layouts, 103 on a public and 206 on a private leaderboard. The pipeline applies layout-specific values of scale and pixel aspect, resamples each frame to square pixels, segments aponeuroses and fascicle fragments with U-Nets and measures the three readings geometrically; the submitted entry blended its angle and length with public notebooks. Because the score is additive, 65 single-change contrasts from 13 base entries measured each decision on both splits. The primary selected entry scored 0.27608 on the private split, the 69th reported position of 690 teams. Reading every frame with square pixels cost 0.029 public and 0.037 private. Of 20 late-stage corrections, 9 kept the sign of their effect on the private split. An audit of the UMUD expert benchmark found that 26 of its 35 frames share their tissue with training images of both DL_Track_US and the challenge. On the 9 frames with no detected match in either set or orientation, the recipe scored 0.213, two experts against two others 0.218 and DL_Track_US 0.263 (0.209, 0.196 and 0.259 when both raters of a reference pair are required), with no difference established. Frame geometry and the extension rule moved readings as much as the choice of model, and small corrections tuned on about 100 public frames did not carry over.
item.dc:creator: Soheil Kooklan

item.title: From Entropy Source to Stochastic Bit-Stream: Low-Cost Converters for True-Random Stochastic Computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.33686v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Stochastic computing (SC) encodes values as the probability of ones in random bit-streams, which allows arithmetic circuits with very low area and power and a natural tolerance to faults. The accuracy and security of an SC system depend on the quality of those bit-streams. Conventional generators build them from pseudo-random or quasi-random sequences, which are predictable, periodic, and correlated across streams drawn from the same generator. This work proposes three methods for converting the unbiased outputs of a true random number generator (TRNG) into stochastic bit-streams (SBS) with arbitrary target probabilities: a block extraction and comparison circuit, a counter-logic circuit, and a cascaded majority-logic pipeline. All three accept bits from any true- random source and are built from standard CMOS logic. They reach the accuracy of a software random generator for both independent and correlated stream generation, and they support the common SC arithmetic operations with error that falls with stream length at the same rate. Hardware synthesis results show that the converters offer favorable area, energy, and area-delay trade-offs relative to pseudo- and quasi-random baselines. Under injected soft errors, block extraction degrades no faster than the best deterministic baseline. By bridging raw entropy sources and application-ready bit-streams, this work makes true-random SC practical on standard CMOS.
item.dc:creator: Mehran Moghadam, Abu Masum, M. Hassan Najafi, Sercan Aygun, Di Wu

item.title: Distortion-Corrected Diffusion MRI Using Rotated-View EPI and Joint Field-Map/Image Estimation with Gaussian Primitives
item.description: arXiv:2606.31521v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Echo planar imaging (EPI) is the standard acquisition technique for diffusion and functional neuroimaging, enabling rapid imaging but suffering from geometric distortions caused by B0 field inhomogeneities. Existing correction methods first reconstruct distorted images using parallel imaging, then estimate the B0 field and correct the distortion in the image domain. In this sequential process, reconstruction artifacts at high acceleration factors and low SNR at high diffusion b-values degrade B0 estimation and limit the overall correction quality. We propose a physics-informed framework that jointly estimates the B0 field, the distortion-free image, and the shot-to-shot phase directly from k-space data, without depending on an intermediate parallel-imaging reconstruction. All three are represented as superpositions of Gaussian primitives embedded within an EPI forward model; the explicit, continuous parameterization captures both smooth regions and tissue boundaries and is evaluated on rotated sampling grids without resampling. The diffusion-weighted image is modeled as real and non-negative, with the image phase absorbed into a per-shot phase factor. Acquiring the blip-up/blip-down data at several phase-encoding orientations, the rotated-view principle of PROPELLER applied to full-FOV single-shot EPI, distributes distortions across orientations, improving point spread function isotropy and providing stronger constraints for B0 estimation. On in vivo brain diffusion EPI at R=4 and 5, the proposed method attains the closest brain-boundary agreement with a distortion-free structural reference, with the largest improvement over sequential methods at high b-value.
item.dc:creator: Wenqi Huang, Zhitao Li, Nan Wang, Yimeng Lin, Mengze Gao, Yurui Qian, Sevgi Gokce Kafali, Xiaozhi Cao, Kawin Setsompop, Daniel Rueckert, Congyu Liao

item.title: PIRA: Pan-CDN Intra-video Resource Adaptation for Short Video Streaming
item.description: arXiv:2510.18606v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In large scale short video platforms, CDN resource selection plays a critical role in maintaining Quality of Experience (QoE) while controlling escalating traffic costs. To better understand this phenomenon, we conduct in the wild network measurements during video playback in a production short video system. The results reveal that CDNs delivering higher average QoE often come at greater financial cost, yet their connection quality fluctuates even within a single video underscoring a fundamental and dynamic trade off between QoE and cost. However, the problem of sustaining high QoE under cost constraints remains insufficiently investigated in the context of CDN selection for short video streaming. To address this, we propose PIRA, a dynamic resource selection algorithm that optimizes QoE and cost in real time during video playback. PIRA formally integrating QoE and cost by a mathematical model, and introduce a intra video control theoretic CDN resource selection approach which can balance QoE and cost under network dynamics. To reduce the computation overheads, PIRA employs state space pruning and adaptive parameter adjustment to efficiently solve the high dimensional optimization problem. In large scale production experiments involving 450,000 users over two weeks, PIRA outperforms the production baseline, achieving a 2.1% reduction in start up delay, 15.2% shorter rebuffering time, and 10% lower average unit traffic cost, demonstrating its effectiveness in balancing user experience and financial cost at scale.
item.dc:creator: Chunyu Qiao, Tong Liu, Yucheng Zhang, Zhiwei Fan, Pengjin Xie, Zhen Wang, Liang Liu

item.title: MedImgAnnotator: batch wise medical image annotation and preprocessing tool
item.description: arXiv:2611.22450v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: The curation of large cohort datasets for developing deep learning models demands annotating or editing over the AI-predicted labels. However, openly available annotation tools are time-consuming, as they involve complex navigational steps and do not support batch processing. This study aimed to develop a simple, fast, semiautomated batch-annotation tool named MedImgAnnotator. The tool was created by integrating editing tools, image mask pair matching logic, preprocessing functions, object detection tool, and a plugin management system. Its performance was evaluated in terms of active annotation time and ease of use by the developer and 12 users using open-source MR and CT scans. Additionally, the tool had been used by the MICCAI 2026 CARE Challenge liver segmentation best performance winner to annotate liver masks from 6412 MRI volumes. The evaluation results showed that MedImgAnnotator reduced active annotation time from 206.5+/-32.87 (average active annotation time of openly available tools) seconds to 59 seconds. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test of 12 users evaluation results recorded P values of 0.032 and 0.008 for the active annotation time and higher ease of use rating metrics, respectively, indicating that the current tool significantly reduces annotation time and enhances ease of use. Moreover, the tool utilization for annotating different regions of interest from different modality scans and body regions shows its usability across modalities and areas of interest. MedImgAnnotator, which significantly reduces active annotation time for large imaging cohorts, is available as an executable file and as a Python script. Access link: https://ewunateassaye.github.io/developed-tools/medimgannotator.html
item.dc:creator: Ewunate Assaye Kassaw, Amit Mehndiratta, Peush Sahni, Anup Singh
